title: A Partial History of Action Figures
summary: Josh and Chuck trace the history of action figures, starting with Barbie's influence and Stan Weston's idea for a soldier doll at Hasbro, which led to G.I. Joe (1964) as the first action figure. They cover Joe's 1960s decline during Vietnam and rebranding as an adventurer, Mego's superhero and Planet of the Apes lines and its loss of the Star Wars license, Kenner's Star Wars figures, and the G.I. Joe cartoon of the early 1980s. They tie the cartoon boom to the FTC's late-1970s children's advertising inquiry, which was dropped after Reagan's appointee and Reagan's veto of a children's TV bill. The episode also covers how figures are sculpted, molded, assembled and packaged, and the collector market for rare figures such as Yak Face, the chokable Boba Fett and telescoping lightsabers. It closes with a listener mail plugging Kiva micro-lending and the team's progress.

segments.title: Opening banter and episode setup
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode on action figures, linking it to the earlier Barbie episode and noting Barbie's role in inspiring action figures.

segments.title: Stan Weston, Don Levine and the soldier doll idea
segments.summary: Stan Weston pitched a soldier doll idea to Hasbro's Don Levine, who coined the term action figures; Weston was reportedly paid $100,000 (about $782,000 today). They discuss how Barbie's accessories drove sales and how toy companies wanted a doll for boys.

segments.title: G.I. Joe debut and early design
segments.summary: G.I. Joe debuted before Christmas as a twelve-inch figure with about 21 to 29 moving parts. G.I. Joe was the collective name for four Armed Forces figures, and the figures were identical apart from clothing. The hosts discuss the scar and inverted thumbnail that helped Hasbro pursue copyright claims against knockoffs, and the Defenders line.

segments.title: G.I. Joe packaging, accessories and the 1960s decline
segments.summary: Packaging showed other figures to encourage collecting, and accessories such as a jet pack, a one-man submarine and an all-terrain vehicle were sold. G.I. Joe sales fell during the Vietnam War, and the line was retired and rebranded as an adventurer.

segments.title: Mego's superhero and movie lines
segments.summary: With G.I. Joe gone, Mego released the World's Greatest Superheroes line in 1972, licensing DC and Marvel characters together, including villains and side characters. Mego also released Planet of the Apes and Star Trek lines and place sets. Montgomery Ward had an exclusive on non-costumed versions of heroes.

segments.title: Mego passes on Star Wars and Kenner takes it
segments.summary: The hosts recount the story that Mego declined the Star Wars license and Kenner picked it up, with competing versions of the story; the hosts note the anecdote comes from a single blog source and ask for verification.

segments.title: Smaller figures and the 3 3/4-inch scale
segments.summary: Mego's Star Trek and superhero lines were eight inches; Takara and Action Man licensed G.I. Joe internationally, and during the oil crisis smaller 3 3/4-inch figures were developed, such as Microman in 1974. The hosts debate whether the big or small G.I. Joes were better.

segments.title: G.I. Joe cartoon and the FTC children's advertising fight
segments.summary: The G.I. Joe cartoon in the early 1980s gave characters names and created an ongoing Cobra storyline. The hosts describe the late-1970s FTC inquiry into advertising to children, industry opposition, Reagan's appointment of a new FTC chairman, and Reagan's veto of a children's programming bill that limited ad time.

segments.title: Star Wars figures from Kenner
segments.summary: Kenner's three and three-quarter-inch Star Wars line launched in 1978 and sold about 40 million units a year, roughly 300 million across its original run. The hosts recall their childhood collections and the big Star Wars dolls.

segments.title: Later action figure boom and collector-driven manufacturing
segments.summary: The hosts describe later figure lines such as Transformers and Marvel and DC figures, and figures based on movies and politicians. They discuss claims that companies release limited runs with errors to create collector value, which they treat as unverified.

segments.title: How action figures are made
segments.summary: The process starts with a sculptor building a wire armature and clay model, taking about two weeks; the head is often sculpted separately. Molds take about two-thirds of production time, and plastics include ABS, polypropylene and polyethylene. Rotational molding avoids seams but loses detail, while injection molding gives finer detail. Figures are assembled, painted and packaged.

segments.title: Rare and valuable Star Wars figures
segments.summary: The hosts discuss collectible rarities: Yak Face, a limited-release figure from the Power of the Force line; the Vinyl Cape Jawa and cloth-caped figures; the chokable Boba Fett that shot a missile and was redesigned; and the double-telescoping lightsabers. Values are mentioned as reported online and treated as unverified.

segments.title: Kiva micro-lending plug and listener mail
segments.summary: A listener writes about making a Kiva micro-loan and how loans are repaid and reinvested. The hosts describe the stuff you should know Kiva team, its membership and total loaned, and invite people to join.
topics: stuff you should know Kiva team

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck list social media and contact details and sign off.
